newsitem.title: SYRIA: Syrian radio renews blaming Israel for blast.
newsitem.headline: Syrian radio renews blaming Israel for blast.

text.p: Syria's state-run radio on Friday renewed accusations that Israeli agents were responsible for the bombing of a bus in central Damascus that killed nine people and wounded 44.
Damascus radio linked Tuesday's bombing to recent attacks on Syrian targets in Lebanon and said it was aimed at forcing Syria to change its position on peace talks with Israel.
"The Israeli fingerprint is clear in the timing and aims of the cowardly terrorist action against the transport bus in Damascus," it said in a commentary.
Israel on Friday condemned the Damascus bombing and rejected the Syrian accusations first made on Thursday. The United States warned Syria against blaming others without providing evidence.

"The prime minister (Benjamin Netanyahu) said that the accusations published in Damascus accusing Israel of responsibility for terrorist attacks in Syria are an outright lie. We have no connection to the terrorist attack in Syria and Syria knows it," the Israeli cabinet said in a statement released after its weekly meeting.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters in Washington on Thursday: "It is a very serious charge for one state to accuse another of actually sponsoring bombings in its capital...It's a wild and irresponsible charge if in fact it is not backed up by evidence."
Damascus radio said: "Israel revived contacts with its defeated agents in Lebanon and asked them to carry out sabotage operations to spoil stability in Lebanon and to harm the good ties with Syria."
"Those agents committed crimes against innocent civilians and a bus in Lebanon and lately a bus in the heart of Damascus," the radio said.

Last month there were two attacks on Syrian targets in Lebanon. Leaflets distributed in Beirut condemned Syria's military presence in Lebanon and criticised Lebanon's pro-Syrian government. The Lebanese government said Israeli-linked hardline Christians were behind the attacks and leaflets.
Syria is the main foreign power-broker in Lebanon where it has some 35,000 troops. Israel occupies part of south Lebanon.
In a Damascus hospital on Friday, survivors described the horror of the New Year's Eve explosion.
Ramadan Sido, 36, told Reuters from his hospital bed that he was walking near the bus station thinking about the presents he wanted to buy his seven children for the New Year.
"Suddenly a big explosion rocked the place and something... slapped my face," he said. "I saw a huge ball of fire...I thought there was a tremor and it was my end." He suffered a broken hand.

Mohammed Osou, a 22-year-old soldier on leave from his Damascus-based unit who was preparing to travel to the northern city of Aleppo to join his family for the New Year, was among the last to board the bus.
"The only empty place was in the back seat and the explosion took place in the middle of the bus at the luggage place...That is why I survived with light wounds," Osou told Reuters.
Syria first reported the explosion on Thursday when an official spokesman blamed Israeli agents. He said Israel wanted to kill the Middle East peace process.
Ties between Syria and Israel, who have held sporadic peace talks since 1991, deteriorated severely after Netanyahu took office in June last year.
Syria has said it will not resume the talks, suspended in March by Israel's previous government, until Netanyahu changes his policy of refusing to swap occupied Arab lands for peace.
